title: Smile to brighten
purpose: Hear what a small smile does to your voice: spread lips shorten the space your voice sounds in, which can make it brighter.
instructions: Say an everyday phrase your usual way.
Say it again with a small smile, as if you're pleased to see someone.
Play the two back to back. Notice how the smiling one sounds, and how it felt to say.
During the day, let a little of that smile into real conversations and notice what changes.

primary_cue.text: Say it with a small smile.

cues.text: Say it with a small smile.
Smile a bit more as you speak, then compare the two takes again.
Notice how the smiling take felt to say, not only how it sounded.

practice_task.prompt_text: Black coffee, please. How was your weekend?

check_questions.text: Play both takes. Which sounds lighter and brighter to you?
How did speaking with a smile feel?

expected_observations: Spreading your lips shortens the space between your vocal folds and your lips a little. That raises its resonances, so the voice can sound brighter.
common_misunderstandings: Lighter doesn't mean quieter, breathier or whispered.
What matters is how it sounds and feels to you; there's no universal score.
stop_conditions: Anything hurts, feels tight or scratchy, or your voice turns hoarse: that usually means too much, too soon.
Rest your voice and come back another day, starting smaller.
If hoarseness or discomfort lasts or keeps coming back, see a GP, or a speech and language therapist who works with voices.
limitations: Written for Lilt for practising on your own. Lilt can't check your technique, and it doesn't replace a speech and language therapist.
Lilt doesn't measure lightness. Your own listening, take against take, is the evidence.
